tagline: Follow wagon ruts from a Snake River crossing toward Boise.
intro: The Main Oregon Trail Back Country Byway links paved and gravel roads across the sagebrush desert between Glenns Ferry and Bonneville Point, southeast of Boise. The Bureau of Land Management presents this 102-mile backcountry route as a way to see Oregon Trail ruts and reach sections on foot. Its suggested eight-hour trip from Boise includes the state park’s interpretive center and stops along the trail.

The trail from Three Island Crossing to Boise carried the main emigrant traffic during the Oregon Trail’s first ten years. Travelers unable to cross the Snake River followed the South Alternate instead. Freight wagons and stagecoaches later used much of the trail to connect with the railroad in northern Utah, and trail travel continued into the early 1900s.

Begin with the loop from Glenns Ferry to the south-bank bluffs above Three Island Crossing, then return to the state park on the north bank. County roads continue toward Rattlesnake Creek and Canyon Creek Stage Station before reaching Bonneville Point. Near Ditto Creek, large granite boulders and grassier hillsides mark a change in the landscape before the trail descends into the narrow creek valley. At Bonneville Point, trail ruts marked with concrete posts lead into the story of the descent toward the Boise River valley.

moments.title: Three Island Crossing State Park
moments.text: Wagon ruts remain between the Snake River and the park’s History and Education Center. Despite the crossing’s name, emigrants used only two of the three islands to ford the river. Strong currents, deep water and concealed holes made the crossing dangerous and caused drownings. Those who feared the ford continued along the rough, dry South Alternate. The park opened in 1971 to interpret the crossing; the byway loop also reaches an overlook with interpretive signs on the opposite bluff. The center interprets the Oregon Trail with exhibits and a film, while the ruts place the crossing story on the ground.

moments.title: Canyon Creek Stage Station
moments.text: The builders of Canyon Creek’s stone stage station used deer hair to bind its mortar. Built by the Archibald Daniel family in 1874, it had separate buildings for cooking and sleeping. Travelers could obtain meals, water and fresh horses before the station became a home and working farm. A 1976 fire left only the stone walls. Restoration rebuilt walls in 2016 and 2017 and added a roof in 2018. Emigrants called this valley Barrel Creek for its round shape and surrounding rock walls. The grounds were deeded to the Bureau of Land Management in 2015 for preservation.

moments.title: Bonneville Point
moments.text: Concrete posts mark Oregon Trail ruts at Bonneville Point, where the wagon route reached a ridge above the Boise River valley. For emigrants, this was their first view of that valley. The river’s cottonwoods were the first substantial trees along the trail for several weeks. From the ridge, the trail dropped over a succession of benches toward the river. Interpretive signs and historical monuments stand at the point, and the marked ruts are available for hiking. In September 1852, traveler Parthenia Blank recorded a gradual ascent followed by a view of dry grass and trees along the riverbank.

practical: Three Island Crossing State Park: BLM asks drivers to avoid trail access roads when wet or muddy; high-clearance vehicles may be required off the byway. (checked 2026-10-11)
